examples.description: With `headerSpan="full"` the header runs across the window with the trigger at its start, in line with a rail below it; this sidebar collapses off canvas.

examples.name: TitleBarFrame
examples.title: A title bar
examples.description: With `titleBar` and `headerSpan="full"`, the header is the window's title bar: the trigger and a menubar at its start, the title and an action, all small, and the page scrolling below it.

examples.name: TwoSidebars
examples.title: Two sidebars
examples.description: A start and an end sidebar, each with its own trigger, state and rail; content adapts to the rail with `useSidebar('end').isRail`.

examples.name: LoadingFrame
examples.title: The first load
examples.description: The same parts with NavList.Skeleton and the same `persist` key stand in for the frame in a LoadingState until the application's data arrives.

parts.description: The app frame: header, sidebars and main region.
The end of the header, for actions.
The start of the header, for a menu button or a logo.
The loading bar along the top of the frame.
One link that skips to a region.
The skip links, shown on keyboard focus.
A loading bar inside a region rather than the frame.
The moving part of the bar.

components.name: Sidebar
components.summary: A frame's sidebar and its parts, which collapse to a rail of icons or out of view, open over the content, resize and become a drawer on phones, with the trigger that opens and closes it.
useWhen: An application's navigation sits in a column at the start that collapses to icons, or out of view.
A directory, an outline or filters sit in a column beside the page that people open, close and resize.
A settings page has its own sub-navigation beside its content, without the app frame (Sidebar.Provider).

avoidWhen.text: The frame around the sidebars, with the header and the main content.
The destinations inside a sidebar.
Two panes of a page that people resize, such as a list and its detail.
A panel that slides in for a task, such as filters on a phone.

examples.name: Rail
examples.title: Rail
examples.description: - Sidebar.Root: the column, with `side`, `collapsible`, `dockAt`, `peek`, `width` and `resizable`. - Sidebar.Header, Sidebar.Content, Sidebar.Group, Sidebar.Footer: its top row, its scrolling sections, its labelled groups and its bottom row. - Sidebar.Handle: its edge, a window splitter that resizes it and collapses or expands it. - SidebarTrigger: the button that opens and closes it, wherever it is: in the sidebar's header, in AppShell.Header or in a page's own header. - Sidebar.Provider: the state of sidebars and their triggers without AppShell.Root, which provides the same. - useSidebar: a side's state and controls, for content that adapts to a rail or closes the sidebar after a choice.

examples.name: Offcanvas
examples.title: Off canvas
examples.description: Collapsed off canvas, the sidebar leaves the window; its trigger in the header brings it back.

examples.name: EndSidebar
examples.title: At the end
examples.description: AppShell.Aside is the page's region at the end, below the header, here resizable; `SidebarTrigger side="end"` opens and closes it.

examples.name: Resizable
examples.title: Resizable
examples.description: A resizable sidebar with its handle: drag it or use its keys; Enter or a click collapses it, and the frame remembers the width.

examples.name: Groups
examples.title: Groups
examples.description: Groups with headings and an action; in the rail the headings hide and hairlines separate the groups.

examples.name: Standalone
examples.title: Without the frame
examples.description: A settings page's sub-navigation in a Sidebar.Provider, with its trigger in the page's own header.

parts.description: The row with a group's label and action.
The handle that resizes the sidebar.
The sidebar's panel when it opens over the page.
The button that opens and closes a sidebar.
The icons of the trigger's states.
The mark of a sidebar with news.
The surface of menus, popovers, tooltips and lists.
The theme boundary around a popup.

components.name: WindowFrame
components.summary: A window without the app frame's sidebars that draws its own title bar, with its content scrolling below it, or the title bar on its own.
useWhen: An installed web app or desktop shell draws its own title bar over the window (the Window Controls Overlay), for a start page or a simple window.
A title bar on its own, at the top of a window the application lays out itself.

avoidWhen.text: The frame of an application with sidebars, whose header can be the title bar.
A row of a page's actions.

examples.name: StartPageWindow
examples.title: Start page window
examples.description: WindowFrame is a window without the app frame's sidebars, for an installed web app or a desktop shell that draws its own title bar while the system draws the window controls over the page. `WindowFrame.Root` fills the window with `WindowFrame.TitleBar` on top and `WindowFrame.Content` scrolling below it, so the window controls never cover a scrollbar; the keyboard scrolls the content as it would the document. A frame with sidebars is AppShell, whose header can be the title bar too.

examples.name: StickySection
examples.title: Sticky sections
examples.description: Content inside the window sticks at `var(--env-frame-sticky-top)`, the top of the content below the title bar.

parts.description: The window frame: title bar and content.
The content under the title bar.
The center of the title bar.
The end of the title bar.
The row of the title bar's three parts.
The start of the title bar.

components.name: Tree
components.summary: A virtualized tree of rows for large hierarchies, such as file trees, with keyboard navigation and a context menu.
useWhen: A hierarchy people expand and collapse, such as folders and files in a workspace's sidebar.
Thousands of rows, such as a large project's files, which the tree keeps fast by rendering only the rows in view.
Rows people preview with a click and open to keep with a double click, as in a desktop editor.

avoidWhen.text: An application's destinations, such as the pages in a sidebar, one or two levels deep.
A flat list of items, each with its own actions.
Records that share the same fields and that people compare.
Sections of content people show and hide in a page.

examples.name: FileTree
examples.title: File tree
examples.description: The application owns the data. It passes the visible rows in order, flattened, each with its `depth`, and updates them when a row expands or collapses; it also owns the selection and what opening a row does. The tree owns focus, keyboard navigation, type-ahead, scrolling and an optional context menu.

examples.name: ContextMenuActions
examples.title: Actions in a context menu
examples.description: Right-click a row, or press <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>F10</kbd>, for its actions, and the empty area for New document. The buttons above the tree offer the same actions.

examples.name: RowDensity
examples.title: Row density
examples.description: `density="md"` gives the rows more room than the default `sm`, here with counts at the end, a detail and a disabled mailbox. Only the padding changes; the text and icons stay the same.

examples.name: ThousandsOfRows
examples.title: Thousands of rows
examples.description: Expanding every folder makes over 10,000 rows; only those in view are in the document.

parts.description: The chevron that expands an item.
The end of an item, for a count or actions.

components.name: DocumentTabs
components.summary: Editor-style tabs for open documents, which people switch, close, pin and close all; the application renders the active document.
useWhen: People open several documents or files and switch between them, such as in an editor or a workspace.
Tabs open and close as people work, and one may be a preview until it is kept (`preview`, `onPin`).

avoidWhen.text: Switching between a fixed set of views of the same content, such as Overview and Settings.
Destinations in an application's navigation.
Choosing one of a few options or filters.
Items people keep open beside the page, such as drafts.

examples.name: OpenDocuments
examples.title: Open documents
examples.description: DocumentTabs is the strip of open documents above an editor: one tab per document, the active one marked, each with a close button. People switch with a click or the arrow keys, close with the button, a middle click, <kbd>Delete</kbd> or <kbd>Backspace</kbd>, or from a tab's context menu, keep a preview tab with a double click, and, with `onCloseAll`, close all tabs from that menu too. The strip renders only the tabs: the application owns the open documents, the active one and its panel.

examples.name: ManyTabs
examples.title: Many open documents
examples.description: In a narrow pane the strip scrolls sideways, the active tab stays in view, and tabs fade at an edge they run past. Drag a tab to reorder it: a line shows where it will land, and near an edge the strip scrolls with it.

examples.name: CloseAllButton
examples.title: Buttons after the tabs
examples.description: `end` puts the application's own content after the tabs, outside the strip that scrolls and on its hairline, such as a button that opens a new document and one that closes them all.

parts.description: The bar that holds the tabs.
The image that follows the pointer while a tab is dragged.
The actions at the end of the bar.
One tab with its close button.

components.name: PanelDock
components.summary: Panels docked side by side at the bottom of a region, for work beside the page, that minimize to tabs and maximize while their content stays mounted.
useWhen: Items people work on beside the page and switch between, such as drafts, conversations or documents.
Work that must survive being set aside, such as an unsaved draft in a panel people minimize.
Several windows open at once in a workspace, which people minimize, maximize, resize and close.

avoidWhen.text: A task that needs an answer before people go on, or one panel beside the page that inspects it.
Switching between open documents in one place, as in an editor.
A short message about something that happened.

examples.name: DocumentDrafts
examples.title: Document drafts
examples.description: - PanelDock.Root lays out the panels and their tabs and renders each panel's content from `children`. - PanelDock.Header is a panel's sticky header: the title and metadata, the application's actions and the window controls, Minimize, Maximize or Restore, and Close, which `controls={false}` leaves out.

examples.name: MaximizedPanel
examples.title: Maximized panel
examples.description: A maximized panel fills the region behind the open panels, which keep their modes; Restore returns it to the row.

examples.name: MinimizeWhatDoesNotFit
examples.title: Minimize what does not fit
examples.description: With `overflow="minimize"` three panels that can't sit side by side at 20 rem make room: the one active longest ago waits as a tab. It comes back once the region widens.

examples.name: NarrowRegion
examples.title: Narrow region
examples.description: Below `stackBelow` one panel at a time fills the region, here the active conversation, and its tab shows the other.

parts.description: A panel's actions in its header.
A panel's window controls: minimize, maximize and close.
A fact beside a panel's title.
An invisible element that measures the dock's room.
The handle that resizes the dock.
The strip of minimized panels' tabs.
The mark of a tab that asks for attention.
The button that restores a minimized panel.

components.name: Breadcrumbs
components.summary: The path from the top level to the current page, with earlier levels as links or buttons.
useWhen: People move through a hierarchy and need to see where they are and go up, such as folders above a document.
A header or a bar names the current item's place in one line beside its status and actions (`wrap={false}`).

avoidWhen.text: The application's main navigation, such as the pages in a sidebar.
Moving between the items of one level, such as views of the same content.
Previous and next pages of a sequence.
Browsing and expanding a whole hierarchy.

examples.name: DocumentTrail
examples.title: Document trail
examples.description: Breadcrumbs show the path from the top level to the current page, such as a workspace, its folders and the document open in them. Earlier levels are links with `href`, through the `LinkProvider`'s link component, or buttons with `onClick` for applications without URLs; the current page is last, in the primary text color, and never a link. The trail is a navigation landmark around an ordered list, and it supplements the main navigation rather than replacing it.

examples.name: WithoutUrls
examples.title: Applications without URLs
examples.description: Levels with `onClick` are buttons. Pressing one shortens the trail, and focus moves to the folder's title, since the pressed level becomes the current page.

examples.name: OneLine
examples.title: One line in a header bar
examples.description: With `wrap={false}` the trail stays on one line beside a status and an action; the current page is cut short first.

examples.name: LevelWithoutPage
examples.title: A level without a page
examples.description: An entry without `href` or `onClick` is plain text, for a level that can't be opened.

parts.description: The current page, the last crumb.
A crumb that is not a link.
The surface of menus, popovers, tooltips and lists.
The theme boundary around a popup.

components.name: Pagination
components.summary: The range of items shown with previous and next page buttons, small enough for a toolbar.
useWhen: A long list or table read a page at a time, such as reports or invoices.
A list read in batches whose total isn't known yet, such as an activity feed.
A toolbar with little room for paging, beside a search field or filters.

avoidWhen.text: Links between the pages of an ordered sequence, such as the chapters of a guide.
Switching between a few views of the same content.

examples.name: PagesOfAList
examples.title: Pages of AList
examples.description: The application owns the page, the loading and the scroll position. Pagination reports the page a press asks for through `onPageChange`, shows a spinner on the button pressed while the page loads, announces the new range and keeps focus on the button, so people who page from the keyboard stay in place.

examples.name: WithoutATotal
examples.title: Without a known total
examples.description: A list read in batches shows the items on the page; `hasNextPage` says when the list ends.

examples.name: SmallToolbar
examples.title: In a small toolbar
examples.description: `size="sm"` gives the buttons the small control height, as the field beside the pager has, and the field shrinks first. The text variant keeps the toolbar quiet.

examples.name: ApplicationStrings
examples.title: The application's own strings
examples.description: EnvUIProvider's `messages.pagination` sets the strings of every pager inside it, in the reader's language, and its `locale` formats the numbers; `previousLabel`, `nextLabel` and `formatRange` set them for one pager. A pager in a language other than the page's takes `lang`, so assistive technology reads it in that language.

parts.description: One page, previous or next button.

components.name: AccountMenu
components.summary: The signed-in person's menu, opened from their avatar or a row with their name, with a header, a theme submenu and an optional organization submenu.
useWhen: The signed-in person's settings, theme and sign out, behind their avatar in a header or their name at the foot of a sidebar.
The theme choice, System, Light or Dark, in the account's menu rather than a toggle of its own.
Switching organizations from the account's menu, where the frame has no switcher of its own.

avoidWhen.text: A switch between organizations at the top of a sidebar, on its own.
Switching between the light and dark themes with one button.
Actions on an item or a view rather than on the account.

examples.name: ThemeAndOrganizations
examples.title: Theme and organizations
examples.description: AccountMenu is the menu of the person who is signed in. Their avatar, or a row with their avatar, name and e-mail address, opens a Menu whose header shows who is signed in, followed by the application's items. Two submenus come with it: AccountMenu.ThemeSubmenu, the theme choice, which stores itself through a ThemePreferenceProvider, and AccountMenu.OrganizationSubmenu, the switch between the person's organizations. The other items are Menu's own parts.

examples.name: RowTrigger
examples.title: A row at the foot of a sidebar
examples.description: The row shows the name and the e-mail address, and opens the menu above it. The theme submenu here sets a theme the application stores itself, and closes the menu after the choice.

parts.description: The account's name and description at the top of the menu.
The account's description in the header, such as an email address.
The account's name in the header.
The column that holds the header's name and description.
The button that opens the menu.
The account's description in the trigger.
The account's name in the trigger.
The column that holds the trigger's name and description.

components.name: RichText
components.summary: Formatted text people edit as it looks, saved as Markdown with references, and shown again read-only.
useWhen: People write formatted text and see it as it will look, such as meeting notes, a brief or release notes.
Text mentions people, topics or files the application knows, saved with their IDs (references).
Formatted text saved earlier shows again read-only, rendered the same way, such as on a detail page (RichText).

avoidWhen.text: People edit Markdown source directly, with a preview.
Showing Markdown from anywhere, with the full CommonMark syntax, footnotes and plugins.
Plain text over several lines, without formatting.
A message in a conversation, sent with Enter.
A single line of text, such as a title.

examples.name: EditAndPreview
examples.title: Edit and preview
examples.description: - RichTextEditor edits the Markdown, with references people insert by typing a trigger such as @, optional slash commands, attachments the application uploads and links from its own picker. - RichText shows saved Markdown read-only with the editor's own schema, so it looks the same and its references work the same. It renders on a server too. - createRichTextExtensions returns the Tiptap extensions both share, for other Tiptap integrations that need the same schema.

examples.name: SavedContent
examples.title: Show saved content
examples.description: RichText shows saved Markdown read-only. The application opens references and links through `onReferenceClick` and `onLinkClick`.

examples.name: References
examples.title: Mention people and topics
examples.description: Each reference source has a trigger, a name for its list and a lookup. Here a timer stands in for a search on a server, which the signal cancels when the query changes.

examples.name: SlashCommands
examples.title: Slash commands
examples.description: `slashCommands` adds a menu of blocks on /, and the application's own commands after them.

examples.name: UploadsAndLinks
examples.title: Attachments and links
examples.description: `onUpload` makes Attach files upload through the application, and `onRequestLink` replaces the link dialog with the application's own picker.

examples.name: EditorCommands
examples.title: Commands from outside
examples.description: `ref.editor` is the Tiptap editor, so the application can change the document with its commands.

examples.name: ReleaseNotesForm
examples.title: In a form
examples.description: With `name`, the form submits the Markdown. `error` says what to fix.

parts.description: A reference to a person or an item.
The list of suggestions while typing a reference.
The well around the toolbar and the document.
The editor's status line, such as a character count.
The row anatomy of menu, select and combobox options.
The end of a row, for a shortcut or a check.
The check of a chosen row.
The column with a row's label and description.
A list of options in a popup.
The message when there are no options.
Long-form text: paragraphs, lists, headings and tables.

components.name: Markdown
components.summary: Renders a Markdown string in envUI's typography and code, and MarkdownEditor writes one with a toolbar and a preview.
useWhen: Content written in Markdown is shown, such as a saved description, a note or a document.
People write formatted prose as Markdown, with a toolbar and a preview of the result (MarkdownEditor).

avoidWhen.text: Plain text over several lines, without formatting.
Formatted text edited as it looks, without visible Markdown syntax.
A message in a conversation, sent with Enter.
Source code to read or copy on its own.

examples.name: ProjectNote
examples.title: Project note
examples.description: MarkdownEditor writes such a string: a native textarea with a formatting toolbar, undo and redo, and a Preview tab that renders with Markdown. Both come from `@envsemble/envui/content`.

examples.name: EditDescription
examples.title: Write and preview
examples.description: MarkdownEditor with a label and a description grows with its text; the Preview tab renders it two heading levels down, as the page that shows it will.

examples.name: OpenInPanel
examples.title: Open links in a panel
examples.description: `renderLink` opens document links in a panel with a plain click, and leaves modified clicks and other links to the browser.

examples.name: CustomElements
examples.title: Render an element your way
examples.description: `components` replaces how an element renders: here a quote becomes an Alert.

examples.name: LinkPicker
examples.title: An application's link picker
examples.description: `onRequestLink` lets the application choose the link, here after a pause that stands in for its picker, with a shorter toolbar.

parts.description: The Markdown source shown as text.
The region that scrolls a wide table.
The editor's status line, such as a character count.
Long-form text: paragraphs, lists, headings and tables.

components.name: Code
components.summary: Inline code in text, highlighted code blocks with a copy button, and the changes between two versions of a file.
useWhen: Text names a command, a value, a file or an identifier, such as `npm run build` (Code).
Source, commands or output of several lines are shown to read or copy, such as an install step (CodeBlock).
People review the changes between two versions of a file, such as a draft against its saved version (CodeDiff).

avoidWhen.text: Keys of a shortcut.
Formatted text written in Markdown, such as notes or a description.
Text people edit, such as a configuration in a form.
The size of a change without its lines.

examples.name: InstallSteps
examples.title: Install steps
examples.description: - Code is inline code inside a sentence, from `@envsemble/envui/content`. - CodeBlock shows source of several lines, highlighted for its `language`, with an optional label and copy button, from `@envsemble/envui/content`. - CodeDiff shows the changes between two versions of a file, rendered by Diffs, and countDiffLines counts the lines they add and remove, from `@envsemble/envui/diff`.

examples.name: HighlightedSource
examples.title: Highlighted source
examples.description: `language` highlights the source, and the label names the file. Copying writes the original string.

examples.name: WrapLongLines
examples.title: Wrap long lines
examples.description: With `wrap` long lines wrap inside the block; copying keeps their original line breaks.

examples.name: PlainOutput
examples.title: Plain text
examples.description: Without a language, such as for a command's output, the source stays plain text.

examples.name: SettingsDiff
examples.title: Code diff
examples.description: CodeDiff shows what a draft changes in a file, and countDiffLines counts its lines for a DiffStat beside the title.

parts.description: The announcement that the code was copied.
The block's heading, such as a file name.
The diff of two versions of code.

components.name: Badge
components.summary: Small static pills that name a state in its tone or a piece of metadata, show a count, or the size of a change.
useWhen: A short state sits beside the content it describes, such as In review, Blocked or Archived.
A short name or category marks an item, such as a team or a folder (`variant="outline"`).
A piece of neutral metadata sits beside related content, such as a plan or a count of seats.
A number belongs to a label, such as unread messages beside a navigation item or comments on a button (CounterBadge).
The size of a change shows beside a file or a version, such as +12 −3 (DiffStat).

avoidWhen.text: An action, or a choice people turn on and off, even when it looks like a pill.
Choosing one of a few filters or views.
A message about a page or section that needs a sentence.
How full or complete something is, such as storage used.
A headline number with its label and trend, such as on a dashboard.

examples.name: ProjectStatus
examples.title: Project status
examples.description: - CounterBadge shows a count, such as unread messages beside a navigation item, with a full name for assistive technology. - DiffStat shows the size of a change in one pill, such as +12 −3, with additions in the success tone and deletions in the danger tone.

examples.name: Tones
examples.title: Tones
examples.description: Each tone carries a meaning; the word says it too.

examples.name: Emphasis
examples.title: Emphasis
examples.description: Soft badges suit most states; a solid badge stands out for the one state that must, and outline badges mark names and categories.

examples.name: NeutralMetadata
examples.title: Neutral metadata
examples.description: A neutral badge holds a fact about the content beside it, such as the plan a card describes or its seats, in place of 0.x's InfoChip.

examples.name: WithIcon
examples.title: With an icon
examples.description: A decorative icon before the label repeats the state at a glance.

examples.name: NavigationCounts
examples.title: Counts in navigation
examples.description: A CounterBadge as a NavList.Item's `end` content, with an `aria-label` that says what it counts; the accent tone marks the count that needs attention.

examples.name: CountsInButtons
examples.title: Counts in buttons
examples.description: In a button, a CounterBadge keeps its own pill and a DiffStat sits on a pill toward the canvas; on a primary button they take the button's text color as an outlined pill.

examples.name: ChangeSize
examples.title: The size of a change
examples.description: DiffStat beside each changed file, read as "124 added lines and 37 removed lines".

parts.description: The badge: a small pill label.
The count of added and removed lines.

components.name: Table
components.summary: Semantic data tables on a rounded surface: sorting, resizable columns, selected rows and stacked rows in narrow containers.
useWhen: People compare values across rows and columns, such as invoices by client, date and amount.
People scan, sort or select records that share the same fields, such as files, orders or members.
Figures read best side by side with their totals, such as hours and amounts per invoice.

avoidWhen.text: A few items, each with its own actions, that people don't compare field by field.
A handful of key figures for a dashboard, such as revenue this month.
Items nested inside other items, such as folders and files.
Arranging content in columns for layout, such as a set of summaries.
A spreadsheet that people edit cell by cell and move through with the arrow keys.

examples.name: ProjectStatus
examples.title: Project status
examples.description: - Table.Root renders the table and its scroll region, and holds what applies to every row: its name, density, sticky header, column widths and narrow layout. - Table.Head and Table.Body hold the header rows and the data rows. - Table.Row is a row, which can highlight on hover or be selected. - Table.HeaderCell heads a column, or a row with `scope="row"`, and can sort its column. - Table.Cell is a data cell, with a `label` that names its value while rows stack.

examples.name: NumericColumns
examples.title: Numbers and totals
examples.description: `numeric` cells use tabular figures aligned to the end, so amounts compare down the column. A header cell with `scope="row"` heads the totals row.

examples.name: SortableColumns
examples.title: Sort by a column
examples.description: A header with `onSortChange` becomes a sort button. The application keeps the order, sorts the rows and gives each sortable header its `sortDirection`.

examples.name: SelectRows
examples.title: Select rows
examples.description: A Checkbox in the first cell selects the row; `selected` reports it and takes the selection colors. Every row gets `selected`, `true` or `false`.

examples.name: RowDensity
examples.title: Row density
examples.description: `density` changes only the rows' padding, from `xs` to `lg`; the text stays the same. Buttons in the cells take the small control height at every density.

examples.name: StickyHeader
examples.title: Sticky header
examples.description: The header row stays in view while the rows scroll beneath it. The region needs a height, here from the layout around it.

examples.name: ResizableColumns
examples.title: Resizable columns
examples.description: Drag the boundary at the end of a header, or focus it and press <kbd>←</kbd> or <kbd>→</kbd>; double-click it to restore the starting widths. A name too long for its column ends with an ellipsis.

examples.name: StackedRows
examples.title: Stack rows in a narrow container
examples.description: In a region narrower than `stackBelow`, each row becomes a block titled by its first cell, with the other cells' labels beside their values.

examples.name: SortWhileStacked
examples.title: Sort while rows stack
examples.description: The header row is hidden while rows stack, so `onStackedChange` shows a Select for the order meanwhile. The table and the Select share the same sort state.

parts.description: A cell's column name, shown when rows stack.
The handle that resizes a column.
The region that scrolls the table.
The button that sorts by a column.
An invisible element that measures whether rows stack.

components.name: DescriptionList
components.summary: The facts about one thing, as labels and their values, beside each other or stacked by the list's own width.
useWhen: A page, card or sidebar shows the facts about one item, such as a project's owner, status and dates.
Settings of one item sit beside their labels, each a small control, such as a visibility Select.

avoidWhen.text: Many items compared by the same fields.
Items people open or act on, one per row.
A form that people fill in and submit.
One headline number with its trend.

examples.name: Facts
examples.title: Facts
examples.description: DescriptionList shows the facts about one thing as labels and their values: a `dl` whose items are its terms with their values. Labels are muted and line up in a column as wide as the longest; below 24 rem of the list's own width, each label moves above its value, so a list in a sidebar or on a phone needs no other layout.

examples.name: Stacked
examples.title: Stacked
examples.description: Contact details with long values put each label above its value.

examples.name: WithControls
examples.title: With controls
examples.description: Settings of one item, each a small control beside its label.

parts.description: The list of labels and values.

components.name: Kbd
components.summary: Key caps that show a key, or keys pressed together joined by plus, in text, hints and menus.
useWhen: Text names a key or a shortcut, such as "Press Ctrl+P to open a document".
A hint lists the keys a list or a popup handles, such as a footer that says which keys move, open and close.

avoidWhen.text: The shortcut of a menu item, which also needs to reach assistive technology.
Key hints in the footer of a quick-open dialog.
Code, a command or a file name in text.
A status or a count beside a label.

examples.name: ShortcutsInText
examples.title: Shortcuts in text
examples.description: Kbd shows a keyboard key as a key cap: a small, bordered label with a heavier bottom edge that sits on the baseline of the text around it. With `keys` it shows keys pressed together, such as Ctrl+P, as one key cap each, joined by a plus. Kbd only shows keys; the application handles the shortcut.

examples.name: KeyHints
examples.title: Key hints
examples.description: A footer that names the keys a list handles, one hint after another.

examples.name: ShortcutSequence
examples.title: A sequence of shortcuts
examples.description: Each step of a sequence is a Kbd of its own, with "then" between them; `keys` is only for keys pressed together.

examples.name: PlatformKeys
examples.title: The reader's platform
examples.description: Apple keyboards name the Command key where others use Ctrl. Pass the keys of the reader's platform; Kbd shows what it is given.

components.name: AnimatedNumber
components.summary: A number in text that rolls to its new value when it changes, so a count updated elsewhere is noticed.
useWhen: A count changes while people make choices elsewhere, such as matching results in a button's label.
A figure follows a setting people change, such as seats left or a price per billing period.

avoidWhen.text: A count that doesn't change while people look at it, which is plain text.
A compact count beside a label, such as unread messages.
A headline figure with its label and trend, such as on a dashboard.
How far a task has come.

examples.name: ShowResults
examples.title: Show results
examples.description: AnimatedNumber shows a number inside text and rolls it to its new value when it changes: in from below when it grows and from above when it shrinks. The movement draws the eye to a count that other controls change, such as the number of results on the button that shows them. The text is always the current value, so accessible names and copied text never hold a number on its way.

examples.name: SeatsLeft
examples.title: Seats left
examples.description: The sentence is a status region, so the new count is announced as people change it.

examples.name: CustomFormat
examples.title: A formatted value
examples.description: `formatValue` writes the price as a currency; it rolls up for yearly billing and down for monthly.

parts.description: The number, which animates when its value changes.

components.name: Rating
components.summary: A read-only rating as stars filled in half steps, named once for assistive technology.
useWhen: Showing a rating people gave, such as a review score or the average of many reviews.
A compact summary of quality beside a name in a list, a card or a table row.

avoidWhen.text: Asking someone to give a rating; offer a few labelled choices instead.
Asking for a value on a continuous scale, such as a satisfaction score from 0 to 100.
A measurement within a known range, such as storage used.
A key figure on a dashboard, such as the average score this month.
A state or a category, such as Approved or Featured.

examples.name: ReviewScore
examples.title: Review score
examples.description: A rating shows a score people gave as stars, such as 4.5 out of 5, filled to the value in half steps. It is read-only: it displays a rating and never asks for one. The stars are one image named by the rating, so assistive technology reads it once, such as "4.5 out of 5 stars"; `showValue` adds the number before them for people who scan.

examples.name: Scales
examples.title: Half stars and other scales
examples.description: The stars fill to the value in half steps. `max` sets another scale, such as ten stars.

examples.name: ReviewList
examples.title: A list of reviews
examples.description: In a list of individual reviews the stars are enough; the reviewer's name says whose rating it is.

examples.name: ApplicationLabel
examples.title: The application's own name
examples.description: `messages.rating.label` on EnvUIProvider writes the accessible name, in the reader's language; the provider's locale writes the number, such as 4,5 with a decimal comma in German.

parts.description: The filled half of a half star.

components.name: RelativeTime
components.summary: A moment as text relative to now, such as 3 hours ago, kept current, with the date and time in a tooltip.
useWhen: How long ago or how soon matters more than the exact moment, such as when a report changed or when a review is due.
Activity and lists where times update while the page stays open, such as Draft saved 2 minutes ago.
A string that says how long ago, for a place that takes only text, such as an option label or an accessible name (formatRelativeTime).

avoidWhen.text: A moment people must read exactly, such as a deadline, an appointment or the date of a record; format the date with Intl.DateTimeFormat.
Choosing a date, or a date and time.
Days shown on a month grid.
A count that changes in place, such as seats left.

examples.name: DraftSaved
examples.title: Draft saved
examples.description: `formatRelativeTime` returns the same text as a string, for places that take only text, such as an option label or an accessible name. It runs anywhere, also on a server.

examples.name: PastAndComing
examples.title: Past and coming moments
examples.description: Past moments read "ago" and coming ones "in"; the unit grows with the distance, from minutes to years.

examples.name: Formats
examples.title: Formats
examples.description: `short` and `narrow` shorten the words for tight spaces.

examples.name: ExactDateNearby
examples.title: The exact date nearby
examples.description: Where the date shows beside it, the relative time needs no tooltip.

examples.name: VersionLabels
examples.title: Text for an option label
examples.description: `formatRelativeTime` returns the same text as a string, for places that take only text. The string doesn't update by itself.

parts.description: A time relative to now, with the exact time in a tooltip.
The surface of menus, popovers, tooltips and lists.
The theme boundary around a popup.

components.name: Disclosure
components.summary: A one-line summary that shows and hides optional details below it, on the native details element.
useWhen: Optional guidance or details that most people don't need, such as how a setting works.
Settings that most people leave alone, such as advanced options in a form.
A list of questions whose answers people open one at a time.

avoidWhen.text: Instructions or errors people need to complete a task, which must stay visible.
Switching between views of the same content.
A hierarchy people expand level by level, such as folders.
Details beside a control that close when people move on.

examples.name: VisibilityHelp
examples.title: Visibility help
examples.description: A disclosure is a one-line summary that shows and hides the details below it. It is the native `<details>` element with its `<summary>`, so opening, closing, the keyboard and what assistive technology hears are the platform's. It suits guidance and settings that most people don't need; what they need to complete a task stays visible.

examples.name: FrequentQuestions
examples.title: Questions, one open at a time
examples.description: Disclosures with the same `name` act as one group: opening an answer closes the one that was open.

examples.name: OpenOnError
examples.title: Open on an error
examples.description: Advanced settings stay closed until a field in them has an error; `open` and `onOpenChange` then open the disclosure so the error shows.

parts.description: The disclosure: a summary that shows and hides a panel.

components.name: Avatar
components.summary: A round picture of a person or organization, with the default person picture or initials as fallback, as a button, or overlapping in a group.
useWhen: A person or an organization is pictured beside their name, such as in a list of members or a comment.
The signed-in account opens its menu from a picture in the application's chrome (AvatarButton).
Who is involved matters more than each name where space is short, such as a project's members in a row (AvatarGroup).

avoidWhen.text: A status or a count beside a label.
An icon for a thing or an action, not a person.
Every name of a list of people that should be read.

examples.name: PersonWithName
examples.title: Person with name
examples.description: - AvatarButton is an avatar as a button, such as the account menu's trigger, with a halo on hover, press and while its menu is open, and the name in a tooltip. - AvatarGroup overlaps the avatars of a set of people, with a chip that counts the people it doesn't show and lists them in its tooltip.

examples.name: Colors
examples.title: Colors
examples.description: The eight colors of an avatar without a picture, with initials and with the default person picture; each holds white at 4.5:1 or more.

examples.name: Sizes
examples.title: Sizes
examples.description: Four sizes, from a compact row to a profile page; each is named here, with no name beside it.

examples.name: Fallbacks
examples.title: Pictures and fallbacks
examples.description: A picture covers the circle. One that fails to load shows the default person picture, and an organization shows its initials.

examples.name: ColorsFromNames
examples.title: Colors from names
examples.description: Each name chooses its color, the same wherever the name appears.

examples.name: OwnColor
examples.title: An organization's own color
examples.description: `hue` sets the color, such as an organization's own, instead of the one its name would choose.

examples.name: AccountButton
examples.title: Account menu
examples.description: AvatarButton opens the account menu; its tooltip shows the name and the e-mail address, and its halo stays while the menu is open.

examples.name: ProjectMembers
examples.title: Members in a row
examples.description: Groups on List rows show three or two avatars and count the rest, also people who are counted in `total` but not passed. The ring takes the row's fill.

examples.name: PressableAvatars
examples.title: Pressable avatars
examples.description: With `onPersonClick` every avatar is a button named after the person; a person with `href` is a link. The chip lists the people it hides.

parts.description: The avatar: an image, initials or a figure in a circle.
What shows without an image: initials or a figure.
The fallback that shows a person's figure.
The figure of a person, drawn when there are no initials.
The button that shows an avatar.
The tooltip that names the account.
The count of avatars that don't fit.
The tooltip that names an avatar or the hidden ones.

components.name: Message
components.summary: Conversation entries in a log: compact bubbles for your own messages, full-width content from others.
useWhen: A conversation between the person using the app and others, such as a chat with a person or an assistant.
A thread of comments in the order they were written, each with its author and time.
A reply that streams in or messages that load while people read, which assistive technology should announce politely.

avoidWhen.text: The field where people write and send the next message.
Items people scan, open and act on, such as a list of conversations.
A short notification that comes and goes, such as Message sent.
A message about a page or a section, such as a warning before a form.
Formatted text on its own, outside a conversation.

examples.name: Conversation
examples.title: Conversation
examples.description: MessageList is a log, so assistive technology politely announces messages as they arrive. A Composer below the list writes the next message.

examples.name: DeliveryStatus
examples.title: Delivery status
examples.description: A message that couldn't be sent says so and offers Retry; while it is sent again it shows Sending.

examples.name: FormattedAnswer
examples.title: A formatted answer
examples.description: Markdown inside a message from someone else keeps the full width. A CopyButton in `actions` copies the answer.

examples.name: CommentThread
examples.title: A comment thread
examples.description: Comments by several people read best at full width: each is `from="other"`, with its author and a RelativeTime in the header.

parts.description: The row with the author and the meta.
The time or another fact about the message.

components.name: Stat
components.summary: Labelled key figures for dashboards, with how they changed and over what period, grouped in even columns.
useWhen: The few figures that sum up a view, such as a dashboard's active projects, tasks done and lead time.
A figure with how it changed since an earlier period, such as +12% from last month.

avoidWhen.text: Many values to compare or sort, such as figures for each project.
A quantity within a known range, such as the seats assigned of a plan's five.
A count on a control, such as unread messages on a tab.
A summary people open or act on, with a description and actions.

examples.name: ProjectHealth
examples.title: Project health
examples.description: - Stat.Root is one figure with its `label`, an optional `trend` and an optional `description`. It has no surface of its own. - Stat.Group puts stats on one surface, a pane by default, in as many even columns as fit.

examples.name: TrendTones
examples.title: Good news and bad news
examples.description: Fewer risks take the success tone, a higher error rate the danger tone, and a rising cost that stays within budget the warning tone.

examples.name: OnAPane
examples.title: On a pane
examples.description: On a pane, the group takes the muted background and a smaller padding; the heading names the group.

examples.name: InACard
examples.title: One figure in a card
examples.description: A stat on its own has no surface; a Card gives it one.

parts.description: The row with the trend and the description.
The change since the last period.

components.name: CalendarHeatmap
components.summary: A calendar grid that shades each day by its value, with a tooltip and keyboard access for every day.
useWhen: A count per day over weeks or months shows a pattern, such as activity or deployments, where the pattern matters more than each number.

avoidWhen.text: Exact figures people compare or read one by one.
A headline number with its trend.
Choosing a day.
A share of a known range, such as storage used.

examples.name: Deployments
examples.title: Deployments
examples.description: A calendar heatmap shows a value for each day as a shade of one tone: weeks are columns and weekdays rows, with month names above and a legend below. Higher values stand out more in both themes. Every day is a cell named with its date and value, shown in a tooltip on hover and focus, and the grid is one tab stop that the arrow keys move through. The application passes the values by day; dates are calendar days, independent of time zones.

examples.name: ColorByRank
examples.title: Color by rank
examples.description: `thresholds` from quantiles of the active days make each step hold about as many days, so a few very busy days don't leave the rest pale.

examples.name: ApplicationStrings
examples.title: The application's own strings
examples.description: EnvUIProvider's messages write the legend in the application's words, in the reader's language, and its locale names the months, weekdays and dates; `weekStart={1}` starts the weeks on Monday.

examples.name: CustomTooltip
examples.title: A tooltip of your own
examples.description: `formatTooltip` lays out the tooltip; the day's accessible name keeps its date and value.

parts.description: The heatmap of days over months.
The empty corner above the weekday labels.
One day's cell, filled by its level.
A month's label above the grid.
An empty cell outside the range.
The region that scrolls the grid sideways.
One level's swatch in the legend.
A weekday's label beside the grid.
The surface of menus, popovers, tooltips and lists.
The theme boundary around a popup.

components.name: EmptyState
components.summary: Explains why a region has no content, such as nothing yet, no results or a failed load, and offers the next action.
useWhen: A list, table or page has no content yet, such as before the first project.
A search or filter matches nothing.
Content failed to load and people can try again (`tone="danger"`).
A state takes the place of a whole page's or region's content (`align="center"`).

avoidWhen.text: Content that is on its way, which keeps its layout while it loads.
A message about a page or section that still has its content.
Feedback after an action, such as a failed save.
Work of unknown length in a small area.

examples.name: FirstProject
examples.title: First project
examples.description: An empty state takes the place of content that isn't there: it says why, such as no projects yet, no results for a search or a list that failed to load, and offers the action that resolves it. It has a decorative icon, a title as a real heading, a description and an action. Inside a card, panel or dialog it lines up with the start; in place of a page's or region's content it centres itself in the room it gets.

examples.name: NoResults
examples.title: No results
examples.description: A search that matches nothing explains why and offers to clear the search; a status line announces the count, and clearing returns focus to the field.

examples.name: LoadFailed
examples.title: Failed to load
examples.description: An error state replaces the list that failed to load and is announced; Try again shows its progress until the list arrives.

examples.name: InPlaceOfContent
examples.title: In place of a page's content
examples.description: `align="center"` centres the state in the height of the region it replaces, with a larger, quieter icon; `headingLevel={2}` fits it under the page's title.

components.name: Spinner
components.summary: Work of unknown length in a small area, such as a panel that is updating, as a turning arc.
useWhen: Work of unknown length in a small area, such as a list that updates after a filter changes.
An update to content already shown, beside the content, which stays in place meanwhile.
Content whose shape isn't known while it loads, such as a file's preview (`size="lg"`).

avoidWhen.text: The work that follows a press, such as saving; show it on the button that started it with `pending`.
Content of a known shape while it loads, such as a card or a list.
A task whose completion can be measured, such as an upload.
Loading a page or a route of an application, along the frame's header.

examples.name: UpdatingPanel
examples.title: Updating panel
examples.description: For the work that follows a press, the button that started it shows a spinner itself with `pending`; see Button.

examples.name: Sizes
examples.title: Sizes
examples.description: Small, medium and large spinners (`sm`, `md` and `lg`), each with its own label.

examples.name: UpdatingList
examples.title: A list that updates
examples.description: Choosing another view keeps the tasks shown while the new ones load. A small spinner beside the choice says they are updating, and the list reports `aria-busy`.

examples.name: LoadingPreview
examples.title: Content on its way
examples.description: A large spinner in the middle of a preview's frame, which keeps its size while the file renders.

components.name: Skeleton
components.summary: Placeholders in the shape of content that is loading, in a LoadingState that names the region once.
useWhen: Content of a known shape while it loads, such as a card, a list or a summary.
The first load of a region, so the page keeps its layout when the content arrives.

avoidWhen.text: An update to content already shown, or content whose shape isn't known.
A task whose completion can be measured, such as an upload.
Content that is empty or failed to load.
The application frame before the first page loads.

examples.name: ProjectSummary
examples.title: Project summary
examples.description: Put a region's skeletons in a LoadingState. It names the region once, such as Loading project, and marks it busy, while each skeleton is hidden from assistive technology.

examples.name: MemberRows
examples.title: Rows of a list
examples.description: An avatar and two lines per row. The round avatar is a square skeleton with a 50% radius, and each row's name takes the default emphasis.

examples.name: SettingsRows
examples.title: Rows of settings
examples.description: Placeholders as tall as the rows that replace them.

examples.name: LoadThenShow
examples.title: From placeholders to content
examples.description: Choosing another project shows placeholders in the card's place until it loads; focus stays on the choice.

components.name: Toast
components.summary: Brief feedback after an action, such as Changes saved, at the edge of the window, announced and dismissed after a few seconds or by people.
useWhen: Feedback after an action people started, such as Changes saved or Invitation sent.
An undo right after an action that took effect at once, such as archiving a project.
An action that failed and can be tried again, such as a save that didn't reach the server.
Work that finished in the background, such as an export becoming ready.

avoidWhen.text: A message about the page or a section that stays while the situation lasts, such as a plan's limit.
A decision people make before anything happens, such as confirming a deletion.
A field's value that needs correcting.
How much of a long task is done, such as an upload.
Work that runs after a press, shown on the control that started it.

examples.name: SaveChanges
examples.title: Save changes
examples.description: Put one Toast.Provider near the root of the application. Any component inside it calls useToast for `show`, `dismiss` and `clear`; `show` takes the notification's `message`, `tone`, `action`, `placement`, `dismissible` and `duration`, and returns its id.

examples.name: Tones
examples.title: Tones
examples.description: Each tone has its fill and icon. The danger notification stays until it is dismissed; the others close after five seconds.

examples.name: UndoArchive
examples.title: Undo an action
examples.description: Archiving takes effect at once, and the notification offers Undo. The action restores the project and dismisses the notification with the id `show` returned.

examples.name: RetryAfterError
examples.title: Try again after an error
examples.description: The first attempt fails. The error stays until it is dismissed, and Try again dismisses it and publishes again.

examples.name: ExportReady
examples.title: Work that finished elsewhere
examples.description: `duration: Infinity` keeps a notification until people dismiss it, for work that ends while they may be looking elsewhere.

examples.name: TopCenter
examples.title: Top center and a limit
examples.description: `defaultPlacement="top-center"` stacks notifications downward from the top. With `visibleLimit={2}`, a third reminder hides the oldest behind a count until a newer one closes.

parts.description: The theme boundary around the notifications.
The icon of a notification's tone.
The region that holds the notifications.

components.name: Alert
components.summary: An inline message about a page or a section, in an info, success, warning or danger tone, with an optional action and dismiss button.
useWhen: A message about a page or a section stays until it no longer applies, such as a paused sync or a blocked release.
Something that just happened failed and the message should stay beside what it concerns, such as a save that didn't go through (`announce`).
A section needs a warning before people act in it, such as storage that is almost full.

avoidWhen.text: Brief feedback after an action, such as Saved or Invitation sent.
A region without content yet, such as an empty list or no search results.
An error about one field of a form.
A status beside a label, such as Draft or Blocked.
A decision people must make before going on.

examples.name: BlockedRelease
examples.title: Blocked release
examples.description: An alert is a message about a page or a section that stays in place, above the content it concerns, until it no longer applies. Its tone sets the tint, the border and the icon; the text stays in the primary text color, so the message reads the same in every tone. An alert can hold an action for the next step and a dismiss button, and it chooses its live role by tone: info and success alerts are polite status messages, and warning and danger alerts interrupt only with `announce`.

examples.name: Tones
examples.title: Tones
examples.description: Info for something to know, success for a result that stays relevant, warning before a problem and danger after one.

examples.name: SaveFailed
examples.title: Announce a failure
examples.description: A save that fails shows a danger alert with `announce`, so it is read at once. Dismissing it moves focus back to the button that saves.

examples.name: CustomIcon
examples.title: Another icon, or none
examples.description: `icon` replaces the tone's icon with one that says more, and `icon={false}` leaves it out for a short message.

parts.description: The alert: an icon and a message in its tone.
The alert's action, such as a button.
The column that holds the title and the message.
The button that dismisses the alert.
The icon of the alert's tone.

components.name: Dialog

Content needs more room than a popup, such as a table, a comparison or a longer form (`width="lg"`).
A search-like task shows results that grow below its field (`placement="top"`).

avoidWhen.text: Confirming one action in place that cannot be undone, such as removing a member from a list.
A question before one action, with Cancel and a button that names the consequence.
Details or a few fields beside the control that opens them.
Feedback after an action, such as Saved or Invitation sent.
A message about the page or a section that stays in place, such as a warning.
Quick open of a document or a command by name.
An item's details, settings or filters in a full-height panel at the edge of the window.
Items people keep open and work on beside the page, such as drafts.

examples.name: ProjectDetails
examples.title: Project details
examples.description: DialogClose is a button inside a dialog or a drawer that closes it, for actions other than the built-in close button, such as Don't save or Done.

examples.name: ConfirmDelete

examples.name: InviteMember

examples.name: ChangeRole
examples.title: A choice
examples.description: RadioGroup rows hold a choice, which takes effect when people save it.

examples.name: RemoveWorkspace
examples.title: Typed confirmation

examples.name: UnsavedChanges

examples.name: ReviewChanges

examples.description: `width="lg"` gives a table or a comparison 44 rem.

examples.name: FindPlan
examples.title: Near the top

The backdrop behind a modal dialog.
The dialog's content between the header and the actions.

The theme boundary that covers the window under a dialog, a sheet or the command palette, so they measure the window and cover the viewport.

examples.name: NavigationDrawer

It is an alert dialog, built on Base UI's alert dialog with Dialog's surface, heading and actions, so it interrupts: it traps focus and a press outside doesn't close it. `onConfirm` runs the action; when it returns a promise, the dialog waits for it, pending, and closes once it resolves.

components.summary: A quick-open dialog near the top of the window, with a search field over a list the application filters and ranks.
useWhen: People jump to a document, a page or a person by name, from anywhere in the application.
People run a command by name, such as one that has no visible control or a shortcut they don't remember.

avoidWhen.text: Choosing a value for a form field from a long list.
A short list of actions behind one control.
Searching or filtering the content on the page.
A task with fields and a decision.

examples.name: GoToDocument
examples.title: Go to document
examples.description: Open it from a SearchTrigger: the trigger shows where search is, shows its shortcut, ⌘K or Ctrl+K, and presses itself when the shortcut is pressed, so its `onClick` is the one place that opens the palette. Closing the palette returns focus to the trigger.

examples.name: RunCommand
examples.title: Run a command
examples.description: Commands with shortcuts as Kbd keys and a Badge as end content, under one group, with a footer.

parts.description: The footer with the keyboard hints.
The row with the search input.
The message when nothing matches, and its announcement.
The row anatomy of menu, select and combobox options.
The end of a row, for a shortcut or a check.
The check of a chosen row.
The column with a row's label and description.

components.name: Menu
components.summary: Actions, destinations and the shared organization switcher, opened from a trigger or a right click.
useWhen: A short list of actions behind one control, such as a row's or a toolbar's More actions.
A few destinations that share a trigger, such as the account pages behind the avatar.
Options that change a view, such as a sort order or whether hidden files show, as radio and checkbox items.
Actions for an area or its rows on right click, beside the visible controls that offer them too (ContextMenu).
Switching between the organizations a person belongs to, in the application shell (OrganizationSwitcher).

avoidWhen.text: The signed-in person's menu, with its header and theme submenu.
Choosing a value for a form field.
An application menubar, such as File, Edit and View.
Searching for and running one of many commands.
An application's navigation, such as the pages in a sidebar.
Content people work in beside a trigger, such as a small form or a color picker.
Switching between views of the same content.
One or two actions that fit beside the content they act on.

examples.name: AccountMenu
examples.title: Account menu
examples.description: The signed-in person's menu, with a header, the theme and the organizations, is AccountMenu, built from these parts.

examples.name: IconsAndShortcuts
examples.title: Actions with icons and shortcuts
examples.description: An icon-only trigger opens actions with icons, shortcut hints, a count and a disabled item whose description says why. Choosing an action runs `onClick` and closes the menu.

examples.name: Destinations
examples.title: Destinations
examples.description: Items with `href` are links through the `LinkProvider`. `target` and `rel` open one in a new tab, and its description says so.

examples.name: GroupsAndSeparators
examples.title: Groups and separators
examples.description: Menu.Group puts related items under a small heading; Menu.Separator splits sets without one. Each set keeps the large outer corners.

examples.name: Choices
examples.title: Radio and checkbox items
examples.description: A radio item checks one choice and closes the menu; checkbox items toggle and keep it open, so several options can change.

examples.name: Submenus
examples.title: Submenus
examples.description: A submenu opens beside its row on hover, or with <kbd>→</kbd>, and choosing an item in it closes every menu.

examples.name: FileMenu
examples.title: A file menu
examples.description: A desktop file menu with shortcuts, a submenu and a group of choices. Labels line up whether a row has an icon, a check mark or neither.

examples.name: ContextMenuForRows
examples.title: Context menu
examples.description: ContextMenu offers actions for the row under the pointer, or for the focused row with <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>F10</kbd>, and New document on the empty space. Each row's More actions button offers the same actions.

examples.name: SwitchOrganization
examples.title: Organization switcher
examples.description: The shared switcher fits the context area of the application shell's sidebar. The active organization is checked, each one shows the person's role, and the create action ends the menu.

examples.name: FirstOrganization
examples.title: Before the first organization
examples.description: Without organizations, the switcher is only the create action, which here creates the first one.

parts.description: The header at the top of the menu.
The place for a chosen item's check.
The check of a chosen item.
The end of an item, for a shortcut or a chevron.
The column with an item's label and description.
The chevron of an item that opens a submenu.
An item that opens a submenu.
The item that creates an organization.
The button that opens the switcher.
The current organization's name in the trigger.
The surface of menus, popovers, tooltips and lists.
The theme boundary around a popup.

components.name: Menubar
components.summary: A desktop-style menubar of menus, such as File, Edit and View, with shortcuts, submenus and access keys.
useWhen: A document-centred application has many commands, grouped as a desktop application groups them, such as File, Edit, View and Help.
A window draws its own title bar and holds the application's menus at its start (with WindowFrame.TitleBar, or AppShell.Root's `titleBar`).

avoidWhen.text: A short list of actions behind one control.
Destinations in an application's navigation.
Running a command by name.
A row of actions that stay visible, such as a toolbar.

examples.name: NotesMenubar
examples.title: Notes menubar
examples.description: - Menubar.Root is the row, named by `aria-label`. - Menubar.Menu is one trigger and its menu, holding Menu.Item, Menu.Submenu, Menu.Group, Menu.RadioGroup, Menu.CheckboxItem and Menu.Separator.

examples.name: InTitleBar
examples.title: In a title bar
examples.description: A window that draws its own title bar holds the menubar at the start of `WindowFrame.TitleBar`, beside the document's name and its actions.

parts.description: The underlined access key in a trigger's label.
A button that opens a menu.
The surface of menus, popovers, tooltips and lists.
The theme boundary around a popup.

components.name: Tooltip
components.summary: A short label beside a control on hover and keyboard focus, such as an icon-only button's name or why a control is disabled.
useWhen: Showing an icon-only control's name, such as a toolbar's Refresh button, for people who don't recognise the icon.
Saying why a control is disabled, such as All seats are assigned, beside the page's own account of it.
Showing a control's keyboard shortcut, such as Bold (Ctrl+B).

avoidWhen.text: A preview of a person, a page or an item, with more than a line of text, on hover or focus.
Content people interact with, such as a small form or a list of choices.
Guidance people need to fill in a field, such as a format or a limit.
Information people need that should stay visible, such as a warning about a limit.

examples.name: IconActions
examples.title: Icon actions
examples.description: While it is open, a control with a name of its own is described by the tooltip, so assistive technology reads the tooltip after the name; a tooltip that only repeats the name adds nothing. Touch screens don't show tooltips, so the control's accessible name or the page says what matters.

examples.name: MenuTrigger
examples.title: Menu trigger
examples.description: An icon-only button that opens a menu or a popover has a tooltip too: the Tooltip is the menu's `trigger`, and passes the menu button's props and ref on to the IconButton. A press opens the menu and closes the tooltip, which stays closed while the menu is open.

examples.name: DisabledReason
examples.title: Disabled control
examples.description: A disabled button keeps its tooltip, through a focusable wrapper. The text below the button says the same for people who can't see the tooltip.

examples.name: ShortcutHints
examples.title: Keyboard shortcuts
examples.description: The tooltip shows the shortcut after the name, below the toolbar; `aria-keyshortcuts` gives it to assistive technology.

examples.name: RailOfIcons
examples.title: Beside a rail
examples.description: `side="inline-end"` opens each tooltip beside a vertical rail of icon buttons, toward the content, also in right-to-left text.

parts.description: The wrapper that lets a disabled control show a tooltip.
The surface of menus, popovers, tooltips and lists.
The theme boundary around a popup.

components.name: Popover
components.summary: A floating panel beside its trigger for details or a small form; Esc or a press outside closes it.
useWhen: Details about something on the page that people open on demand, such as a document's history or what a setting means.
A small form beside the control it changes, such as renaming an item or choosing filters.
An explanation behind an icon button, such as a help mark beside a value.

avoidWhen.text: A short name or hint for a control, shown on hover and focus.
A preview of a link's destination, shown on hover.
A list of actions or destinations.
Choosing a value for a form field from a list.
A task that needs people's full attention or more room, or a consequence to confirm.

examples.name: DocumentDetails
examples.title: Document details
examples.description: A popover is a floating panel that opens beside its trigger, for details people ask for or a small form that changes something nearby. It moves focus into itself as it opens, and closes with <kbd>Esc</kbd>, a press outside or when focus leaves it, so people return to what they were doing. Popover is built on Base UI's popover; it is not modal, so the rest of the page stays usable.

examples.name: RenameInPlace
examples.title: A small form
examples.description: A function child receives `close`: the form renames the document and closes the popover, and Cancel closes it without a change. The `lg` width gives the field room.

examples.name: FilterTasks
examples.title: Controlled filters
examples.description: `open` and `onOpenChange` control the popover: it starts from the filters in use each time it opens, and Apply closes it. The trigger counts the filters applied.

examples.name: FieldHelp
examples.title: Help beside a value
examples.description: An icon-only trigger, named after what it explains, opens the popover to its right with `side="right"`.

parts.description: The surface of menus, popovers, tooltips and lists.
The theme boundary around a popup.

components.name: HoverCard
components.summary: A card of supplementary details that opens beside a link on hover and keyboard focus, like a link preview.
useWhen: A link or a name refers to something people may want a glance at before following it, such as a document's summary or a person's role.

avoidWhen.text: A short hint that names a control.
Details or a small form that people open on purpose and work in.
A task that needs people's attention before they go on.
Information people need to complete a task, which must stay visible.

examples.name: DocumentPreview
examples.title: Document preview
examples.description: A hover card shows supplementary details beside its trigger, usually a link, once the pointer rests on it or keyboard focus reaches it, like a preview of the page the link leads to. It stays open while the pointer moves onto it, so its text can be read and selected. Focus stays on the trigger, and the card is not a dialog. HoverCard is built on Base UI's preview card.

examples.name: PersonDetails
examples.title: A person's details
examples.description: The `lg` card has room for an avatar beside the name and a role, and a line about the person.

examples.name: Placement
examples.title: Above the trigger
examples.description: `side="top"` and `align="start"` open the card above the link, lined up with its start, such as for a link near the bottom of a pane.

parts.description: The card that opens on hover.
The surface of menus, popovers, tooltips and lists.
The theme boundary around a popup.

components.name: Meter
components.summary: A measurement within a known range, such as the seats assigned of a plan or the storage used of a quota, as a labelled bar.
useWhen: A quantity within a known range, such as the seats assigned of a plan's five or the storage used of a quota.
Several limits people compare at a glance, such as a plan's seats, projects and requests.

avoidWhen.text: How much of a task is done, such as an upload or an import.
A key figure without a range, such as the active projects this month.
A value people set within a range, such as a volume or a limit.
A score on a scale of stars, such as a review's 4.5 out of 5.

examples.name: SeatsAssigned
examples.title: Seats assigned
examples.description: A meter shows a measurement within a known range as a labelled bar: the seats assigned of a plan, or the storage used of a quota. It is read-only, and assistive technology reads it as a meter named by its label, with its value and range. For how much of a task is done, use Progress, which shares its look.

examples.name: StorageQuota
examples.title: Units in words
examples.description: The value shows the abbreviation, and `aria-valuetext` reads the unit in words.

examples.name: PlanUsage
examples.title: Limits of a plan
examples.description: Meters of one plan side by side, each with its own range. The text below says what the full one means.

parts.description: The row with the label and the value.
The filled part of the track.

components.name: Progress
components.summary: How much of a task is done, such as an upload, as a labelled bar, or that it runs while the amount is unknown.
useWhen: A task whose completion can be measured, such as an upload, an import or an export.
A task that has started but can't be measured yet, such as preparing an export (`value={null}`).

avoidWhen.text: A measurement within a range, such as seats assigned or storage used.
Work of unknown length in a small area, such as a panel that is updating.
Content of a known shape while it loads, such as a card or a list.
Loading a page or a route of an application, along the topbar.
Saying that a task finished or failed.

examples.name: UploadingFile
examples.title: Uploading file
examples.description: Progress shares its look with Meter, which shows a measurement within a range. For loading a page or a route, AppShell.Root's `loading` shows a bar along its header.

examples.name: ImportContacts
examples.title: Items done of a total
examples.description: `max` is the number of items, and the value counts them; `aria-valuetext` reads it with its unit.

examples.name: PreparingExport
examples.title: Amount unknown
examples.description: `value={null}` shows a sweeping indicator while the task runs and its amount is still unknown.

examples.name: ExportMembers
examples.title: From preparing to done
examples.description: The export starts with an unknown amount, shows the share done once it is known, and ends with a status message in place of the bar. The button stays pending meanwhile.

parts.description: The row with the label and the value.
The filled part of the track.
One segment of a segmented bar.

patterns.name: forms
patterns.title: Form layout and validation
patterns.summary: Ask for information in a form, check it, and help people fix what's wrong.
useWhen: Someone gives or changes several pieces of information at once, and submits them together.
A form refuses what people entered and they need to find and fix each problem.

avoidWhen.text: A single setting that takes effect at once.
Confirming a destructive action.
Filtering a list or a table as people choose.

examples.name: CreateProject
examples.title: Create project
examples.description: Use this pattern to ask for information in a form and get it right on the first submit: one column of labelled fields, the primary action after the last one, and errors that say how to fix each problem, shown when people submit or leave a field, with focus taken to where they need to act.

examples.name: ErrorSummary
examples.title: Error summary
examples.description: Submitting with errors shows each field's error and a summary at the top, which takes focus. Each link in it moves focus to its field. envUI has no error summary component yet: this is a danger Alert with a list of Links, and its title is made a heading by hand. Leave the Alert without `announce`: a danger Alert then has no role, so it is read once, as it takes focus, rather than announced as an alert and read again with focus.

examples.name: ValidationTiming
examples.title: Validation timing
examples.description: A field is checked when people leave it, once they have typed in it, and on submit. While people type, an error only clears, as soon as the value is right. With two fields, a refused submit shows the error summary and moves focus to it.

examples.name: ServerError
examples.title: Server error
examples.description: The first save fails: the fields keep their values, an Alert at the top says what happened and takes focus, and saving again succeeds.

examples.name: GroupedChoices
examples.title: Grouped choices
examples.description: One choice of several is a RadioGroup. Several choices are Checkboxes in a native `fieldset` whose `legend` names them, since envUI has no checkbox group yet.

patterns.name: settings
patterns.title: Settings
patterns.summary: Let people change how the application works for them, and see each change apply.
useWhen: Someone changes a preference that applies at once, such as a notification or the theme.
Someone edits a few related values that only make sense saved together, such as a profile.

avoidWhen.text: Several answers given once and submitted together, such as creating something.
A choice that filters or changes the view of the page people are on.

examples.name: ImmediateToggles
examples.title: Immediate toggles
examples.description: Use this pattern to let people change how the application behaves for them: notifications, privacy, appearance, their profile and the rare action that can't be undone. Each setting either applies the moment people change it or waits, with the settings it depends on, for a Save button, and the two never share a section.

examples.name: SaveSection
examples.title: Save a section
examples.description: A profile's fields depend on each other, so they wait for Save. The section marks its unsaved changes, and Cancel puts back what was saved.

examples.name: AppearanceChoice
examples.title: Appearance
examples.description: The theme applies the moment people choose it, through `useThemePreference`. The density only keeps the choice in the example: the application stores it and passes it to the root provider's `scale`, the app's one scale.

examples.name: DangerZone
examples.title: Danger zone
examples.description: Deleting the workspace can't be undone and affects everyone, so the dialog asks for its name. A confirmation with the wrong name keeps the dialog open and says what to enter.

patterns.name: destructive-actions
patterns.title: Confirmation and destructive actions
patterns.summary: Let people delete, remove or archive with as little friction as is safe, and undo or confirm by what is at stake.
useWhen: People delete, remove, archive or end something.
An action affects other people or can't be undone.

avoidWhen.text: A decision that needs fields or several choices, beyond a confirmation.
Reporting the outcome of an action that people can't change.

examples.name: UndoInstead
examples.title: Undo instead
examples.description: Use this pattern to choose how much friction a destructive action needs. Asking "Are you sure?" before everything trains people to confirm without reading.
